## Assistant
Yes — through the lens of efficiency, the architecture looks much stronger.
The question becomes:
Does this reduce search, attention, training data, invalid actions, debugging cost, or inference cost?\text{Does this reduce search, attention, training data, invalid actions, debugging cost, or inference cost?}Does this reduce search, attention, training data, invalid actions, debugging cost, or inference cost?
And the answer is: yes, plausibly, in several ways.
1. Graph constraints reduce action search
Without a graph, the model chooses among all possible actions:
AallA_{\text{all}}Aall​
With a state graph, it chooses only among legal neighbors:
A(qt)={q′:(qt,q′)∈E}A(q_t)=\{q' : (q_t,q')\in E\}A(qt​)={q′:(qt​,q′)∈E}
So if the full action set has 100 options, but the current state has 4 legal next moves, the classifier has a much easier job:
100→4100 \to 4100→4
That is a major efficiency gain.
This is exactly what the toy run showed: the legality mask removed illegal transitions and improved accuracy.
2. Grammar reduces the dimensionality of judgment
Instead of asking the model:
“What should I do next?”

we ask:
JSON{  "evidence_strength": 0.72,  "contradiction_pressure": 0.31,  "answer_readiness": 0.64,  "search_value": 0.58}
Then deterministic rules interpret the scores.
That changes the task from:
open-ended policy generation\text{open-ended policy generation}open-ended policy generation
to:
typed measurement\text{typed measurement}typed measurement
This is cheaper, more stable, and easier to calibrate.
3. Hyperbolic geometry compresses hierarchy
If the task space is hierarchical, flat embeddings waste dimensions representing tree-like branching.
Hyperbolic space represents trees efficiently because distance grows exponentially with radius.
So for research-agent behavior:
goal→subgoal→source cluster→claim→citation\text{goal}
\to
\text{subgoal}
\to
\text{source cluster}
\to
\text{claim}

\text{citation}goal→subgoal→source cluster→claim→citation
hyperbolic geometry can encode depth and branching with fewer dimensions than a flat Euclidean representation.
Efficiency gain:
less embedding capacity needed for hierarchy\text{less embedding capacity needed for hierarchy}less embedding capacity needed for hierarchy
and:
cheaper nearest-branch / nearest-prototype classification\text{cheaper nearest-branch / nearest-prototype classification}cheaper nearest-branch / nearest-prototype classification
4. Group-action quotienting reduces attention
Dense attention is:
O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2)
because every object can attend to every other object.
If group actions identify equivalent objects, you attend over orbits:
V/HV/HV/H
instead of raw objects:
VVV
So attention cost becomes approximately:
O(∣V/H∣2)O(|V/H|^2)O(∣V/H∣2)
instead of:
O(∣V∣2)O(|V|^2)O(∣V∣2)
If 1,000 objects compress into 100 orbits:
1,0002=1,000,0001{,}000^2 = 1{,}000{,}0001,0002=1,000,000
versus:
1002=10,000100^2 = 10{,}0001002=10,000
That is a 100× relation-space reduction before local re-expansion.
5. IDF tells you where to spend compute
IDF gives a cheap priority rule:
expand rare/high-value structures, keep common structures compressed\text{expand rare/high-value structures, keep common structures compressed}expand rare/high-value structures, keep common structures compressed
So routine states stay coarse:
SearchReadSummarize
but rare diagnostic states get extra attention:
ContradictionWallLoopTrapThreeWayDecisionTieIllegalTransitionPressure
That is efficient because compute is spent on rare high-information regions instead of common low-information flow.
6. Singularity detection reduces wasted loops
A low-margin or singularity detector flags states like:
p(Write)≈p(SearchMore)p(\text{Write}) \approx p(\text{SearchMore})p(Write)≈p(SearchMore)
or:
p(Verify)≈p(ResolveConflict)p(\text{Verify}) \approx p(\text{ResolveConflict})p(Verify)≈p(ResolveConflict)
Instead of letting the agent churn, the controller can trigger a specific recovery action:
ask clarificationretrieve targeted evidenceinvoke verifiersummarize contradictionstop exploration
Efficiency gain:
less wandering+less repeated search+earlier escalation\text{less wandering}
+
\text{less repeated search}
+
\text{earlier escalation}less wandering+less repeated search+earlier escalation
For research agents, this may be one of the biggest practical wins.
7. State machine improves sample efficiency
A neural policy trained from scratch must learn:
legal transitions;
impossible actions;
task phases;
when to stop;
what loops are bad;
how to recover.

A typed graph gives much of that structure for free.
So learning focuses on:
scoring states and transitions\text{scoring states and transitions}scoring states and transitions
not discovering the whole control topology.
That should reduce training data requirements.
8. Debugging efficiency improves
A pure neural controller fails opaquely.
This system can say:
JSON{  "state": "Verify",  "top_next_states": {    "Write": 0.42,    "RetrieveMore": 0.37  },  "singularity": "WriteSearchBoundary",  "reason": "answer readiness and search value are close",  "legal_transitions": ["Write", "RetrieveMore", "ResolveConflict"]}
That is much cheaper to debug than inspecting raw logits or hidden activations.
So the system is efficient not only computationally, but also operationally.
Efficiency summary
ComponentEfficiency gainTyped grammarreduces open-ended reasoning into scored fieldsGraph state machinereduces action search and prevents illegal movesHyperbolic geometrycompresses hierarchy and branchingGroup quotientingreduces all-to-all attentionIDF weightingspends compute on rare diagnostic regionsSingularity detectoravoids loops and unstable indecisionDistribution layerenables cheap uncertainty-aware routingState/history recordsavoids recomputing context from scratch
The strongest efficiency claim
The architecture is best understood as a compute allocation system.
It says:
Use cheap structure for routine control, and spend expensive model attention only where the structure detects ambiguity.\boxed{
\text{Use cheap structure for routine control, and spend expensive model attention only where the structure detects ambiguity.}
}Use cheap structure for routine control, and spend expensive model attention only where the structure detects ambiguity.​
So the efficient loop is:
1. Use grammar + graph for cheap routing.2. Use ML only to score uncertain semantic quantities.3. Use quotienting to compress equivalent objects.4. Use IDF/singularity signals to decide where to expand.5. Use hyperbolic geometry to keep hierarchy compact.
That is a very solid efficiency argument.
The core efficiency slogan is:
Do not ask the model to reason over everything.\boxed{
\text{Do not ask the model to reason over everything.}
}Do not ask the model to reason over everything.​
Make the structure remove impossible, redundant, common, and low-information cases first.\boxed{
\text{Make the structure remove impossible, redundant, common, and low-information cases first.}
}Make the structure remove impossible, redundant, common, and low-information cases first.​

The graph as a reservoir?
The graph itself can also behave like a reservoir if it has recurrent dynamics.
If agent state evolves as:
qt→qt+1q_t \to q_{t+1}qt​→qt+1​
and memory fields update over time:
mt+1=ϕ(qt,mt,Yt)m_{t+1}=\phi(q_t,m_t,Y_t)mt+1​=ϕ(qt​,mt​,Yt​)
then the graph-state machine has temporal memory. If it is rich enough, it becomes a structured dynamical reservoir.
But if the graph is only a static transition mask, then it is not the reservoir. It is the controller or constraint layer.
So:
static graph=constraint/readout structure\text{static graph} = \text{constraint/readout structure}static graph=constraint/readout structure

Hyperbolic geometry as reservoir geometry
The hyperbolic space is not itself the reservoir. It is the geometry of the reservoir state.
It tells you:
where the state is;
how deep it is in the task hierarchy;
whether it is moving toward the boundary;
whether it is near a decision wall;
which graph region it belongs to.

Readout
This experiment says:
Graph constraints are efficient when the classifier would otherwise waste capacity learning impossible transitions.
Typed features help when the scorer has enough context to use them.
Singularity flags are useful because low-margin states are much more failure-prone.
This was not a real BabyAI run and not the full hyperbolic architecture.
The clean takeaway:
The graph is load-bearing when it externalizes structure the model has not already learned.\boxed{
